transcendental dialectic as the ironic destruction, by means of parody, of a metaphysics governed by controlling reason (p. 89 n.);

All three concern me: me, the decisionist; me, the parodist; and me, the propagator of the principle: I do not compare the victims. I compare only the judges! And then there is the motto to the intermediate remark on p. 52, with which I would like to end this year:
The philosophers have changed the world in various ways.
The point, however, is to spare it.
Looking ahead to the coming year 1959 from the end of 1958 (predictions):

After the national component of Bismarck’s National-Liberal Reich became independent under the Hitler regime and was driven to explosion, the liberal component of that Reich is now becoming independent in its turn and being driven ad absurdum.
Perhaps this will happen as early as the coming year.
In Germany, Gelimer’s laughter will spread ever more irresistibly and become impossible to extinguish.
The next bestseller, which will replace Pasternak—and which it will be an unmistakable sign of neo-Nazism not to buy—would be best given the name Rafo Konforti.
This year, many gravediggers will themselves be buried.
Fishing in troubled waters will prove to be child’s play compared with fishing in the hour before the Maelstrom, when the fish are paralyzed by fear.
Khrushchev’s ultimatum has produced just such a paralysis. Above all, the paralysis consists in no longer wishing to distinguish between friend and enemy.

According to the classical rules of the political cycle—as seen in the model case of France—restorations following long coalition wars last fifteen years.
Applied to Germany today, this would mean that the present period continues until 1960.

Or, if we begin counting from 1948 or 1949, until 1963/64. So for the moment we still have a reprieve before the hanging. We shall thoroughly enjoy the condemned man’s last meal and diligently butter our Nuremberg gallows.
So many political trials will be conducted in the Federal Republic of Germany that some just people will finally understand my thesis:
that a trial changes the very object being tried.
Some will also understand why I so often quote the sentence:
I do not compare the victims. I compare only the judges.

And the few who are initiated will understand where the development is heading—a development that does not yet fully take the form of justice being killed by political overburdening, but which already reveals precisely that tendency.
Out of homo homini homo—man is man to man—out of the complete humanization of law, there arises: judex homini lupus. The judge is a wolf to man.

But that does not have to prevent us from seeing our reality. On the contrary: it can and should shake the scenery and stage sets of deception. In that way, it becomes a form of appeal appropriate to the situation:
J’en appelle de ta justice à ta réalité.
I appeal from your justice to your reality.
